summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework on legal gender recognition, health care and hate-crime law. The sources for this jurisdiction contain no city statute of its own and no enforcement figure recorded for the City.

Trans and travesti sex workers in the city face police violence that has become more common since the current national government took office, Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade in reporting published on 10 April 2025. The account supplies no incident counts and no dates for individual cases.

Emergency decree DNU 61/2025, published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. Where it applies, it prohibits a person who has legally changed gender from being held in a women's prison when detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts describe the decree as illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention, so its standing in the City is contested.
tangentialFactors:
At national level, which is the environment a visitor moves through in the capital, Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62% rise year-on-year and a ten-year record of one every 38 hours, according to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026. The figure is a raw national count with no population denominator, and it aggregates sexual orientation with gender identity, so it cannot be read as a per-capita magnitude or as a trans-specific rate.

Of the 2025 total, 32% occurred in police stations and penal facilities, and security-force violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 cases, and most perpetrators were security personnel or unknown assailants. These are national figures; the source gives no breakdown for Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, and the 62.5% share is a composition of the victim total rather than a rate.

The national administration has eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law, according to Washington Blade reporting of 10 April 2025. The same reporting records harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, prohibits gender-affirming interventions for people under 18 nationwide. A Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional in April 2025 and restored access.
localsOnly:
Trans public-sector workers hired under the national Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of posts, have been dismissed by the current administration, according to Washington Blade reporting of 10 April 2025. The measure is national and reaches residents of the City.

People held in detention in Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires fall under DNU 61/2025 only where the City adheres, since the decree invites adherence rather than compelling it. FALGBT and legal experts are challenging the decree as illegal and unconstitutional, so its application to residents held in the City's facilities is unresolved.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires has adhered to DNU 61/2025 is not stated in the sources; the decree invites the City to adhere and the sources record no decision either way.

No city-specific enforcement statistic, hate-crime breakdown or incident count for Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires appears in the sources. The 2025 hate-crime figures are national aggregates and cannot be attributed to the City.

The Washington Blade account of 10 April 2025 reports the direction of change in police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in the city but gives no counts, no dates for individual incidents and no locations within the City, so the prevalence of that violence here is not quantified.

No current city ordinance addressing discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity appears in the sources for this jurisdiction, and the terms of any local coverage are not sourced here.
